revision.title: SEAL Intel: Scaling Actionable Threat Intelligence for Ethereum
revision.summary: SEAL collects threat intelligence through incident response, ecosystem reporting channels, and security research. This grant will connect those workflows into a shared pipeline that validates, enriches, and correlates Ethereum-relevant intelligence, delivering machine-readable feeds, urgent alerts, and actionable defensive recommendations. Over six months, SEAL will test these capabilities with independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations and measure intelligence quality, delivery speed, integration, and documented defensive actions.

sections.why:
Ethereum security teams face high volumes of fragmented threat information across incidents, malicious-domain lists, attacker infrastructure, private reporting channels, on-chain observations, and external research publications. As blockchain security has matured, attackers have increasingly targeted operational infrastructure, developers, credentials, and software supply chains alongside smart contracts, creating a growing need for intelligence that connects these threats to practical defensive actions. These sources differ in structure, reliability, and sharing restrictions. Teams must spend significant analyst time reconciling them before determining whether a threat affects their systems and what defensive action to take.

SEAL already has visibility into incidents and malicious campaigns across the Ethereum ecosystem. This initiative will make that intelligence easier to use through validated records with supporting evidence, relevant alerts delivered to affected teams, and recommendations that specify concrete defensive actions. Participating organizations will be able to integrate intelligence into their existing security tooling and contribute observations through controlled information-sharing channels.
sections.in_scope:
SEAL Intel will expand its existing threat intelligence operations into an automated, analyst-validated service for Ethereum and its Layer 2 ecosystem. The grant funds new integrations, intelligence processing, distribution tools, and partner adoption—not the creation of a new intelligence team.

**1. Collection and normalization**

Build connectors for curated public and permissioned sources, including security research, malicious-domain feeds, incident reports, on-chain observations, and trusted reporting channels. Preserve source provenance, confidence, and sharing restrictions. Extract and deduplicate information from structured and unstructured reports, normalize it using STIX 2.1 with Ethereum-specific indicators (wallet addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, malicious dApp domains), and classify threats by category and affected participant type.

**2. Processing, correlation, and analyst review**

Automate enrichment and correlation against existing SEAL intelligence and incident observations, subject to permissions. Analysts review records before release for correctness (validity, source reliability, false positives), enrichment (supporting evidence and links to infrastructure, incidents, malware, and campaigns), and relevance (affected organizations, urgency, defensive actions). Outputs are evidence-linked, analyst-approved intelligence records. SEAL's differentiator is combining automation with direct incident visibility and researchers experienced in Ethereum threats; the technology reduces repetitive work so analysts can provide actionable guidance rather than raw indicator lists.

**3. Alerts, recommendations, and feeds**

Deliver flash alerts for active threats; tailored defensive recommendations for protocols, exchanges, wallets, and infrastructure providers; periodic campaign and threat reports; and authenticated TAXII 2.1 and REST feeds for integration into existing security tooling. Provide filtering by threat category, participant type, and authorized sharing level, plus API documentation and onboarding guidance.

**4. ISAC collaboration**

Connect selected existing SEAL reporting and ISAC workflows to enable two-way intelligence exchange. Approved participants can submit observations, receive relevant alerts, request context, and coordinate on shared threats. Apply contributor permissions, optional redaction or anonymization, and TLP 2.0 restrictions. Provide contributor feedback where confidentiality permits. This strengthens existing coordination rather than building a new messaging or incident-response platform.

**5. Security and quality**

Implement vetted access, role-based permissions, provenance, TLP-aware distribution, audit logs, and correction or withdrawal procedures for stale or inaccurate intelligence. Protect restricted sources and review automated outputs for false positives and malicious submissions.

**6. Pilot and verification**

Integrate independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations, gather operational feedback, and measure source coverage, extraction quality, analyst effort, alert delivery speed, feed/API usage, contributions, and documented defensive actions. An independent reviewer verifies the quantitative acceptance criteria specified separately in the milestones.

**Use of funds:** The proposed six-month $267,000 budget covers engineering ($108,000), intelligence analysis ($54,000), partner integration ($60,000), delivery management ($15,000), infrastructure ($18,000), and independent review ($12,000), subject to confirmation. Existing SEAL capabilities and previously funded work are excluded from duplicate reimbursement.
sections.out_scope:
The initiative does not include:

- Guaranteed prevention of all exploits, phishing campaigns, or security incidents.
- Replacement of participating organizations' existing security operations or incident-response teams.
- Unlimited custom threat investigations, security assessments, or consulting services for individual organizations.
- Automated changes to participant systems, including credential rotation, patching, or blocking.
- Development of an entirely new endpoint security, blockchain monitoring, messaging, or incident-response platform.
- Expansion into unrelated blockchain ecosystems beyond the agreed Ethereum and Layer 2 scope.
- Redistribution of restricted or confidential intelligence without authorization.
- Private donor services or features not expressly included in the approved grant scope and milestones.

The grant expands SEAL's existing intelligence capabilities and coordination workflows. It does not replace SEAL 911 or create a separate incident-response organization.
sections.team:
Security Alliance (SEAL) will deliver this initiative through its established SEAL Intel program, drawing on its existing intelligence, engineering, security research, and incident-response expertise.

- **Oskar (@blackbigswan) — SEAL Intel Lead:** Responsible for intelligence priorities, technical direction, analyst workflows, research coordination, and overall intelligence delivery. Oskar leads SEAL's existing threat intelligence operations and brings direct experience analyzing threats affecting Ethereum organizations.

- **Joe Dobson (@dobsec) — Security Research and Threat Intelligence:** Formerly of Mandiant, Joe contributes expertise in cybersecurity research, malware analysis, threat actor investigations, and developing actionable intelligence for enterprise and government security teams. His work will support intelligence analysis, enrichment, correlation, and defensive recommendations.

- **Peter Kacherginsky (@iphelix) — Security Research and Intelligence Contributor:** Peter brings cybersecurity expertise across traditional security and Web3. He operates BlockThreat, a security research publication covering blockchain threats, and will contribute specialized research and intelligence expertise on a limited part-time basis. Any use of BlockThreat intelligence will follow applicable permissions and data-sharing arrangements.

- **Matias “Matta” Aereal Aeón (@mattaereal) — Security Frameworks and Technical Research:** Matta leads SEAL Security Frameworks and founded The Red Guild. His expertise in threat modeling, security frameworks, and practical blockchain security guidance will help translate observed attacker behavior into structured, actionable defensive recommendations.

- **Dickson Wu (@DicksonWuML) — On-Chain Security and Incident Response:** Dickson contributes to SEAL Safe Harbor, which supports secure asset recovery during critical protocol incidents. His experience in on-chain security and incident coordination will inform blockchain-specific threat analysis and recommendations for protocols and infrastructure providers.

- **Additional SEAL Engineering and Operations Contributors:** Existing SEAL personnel will support connector development, data normalization, intelligence automation, API/TAXII delivery, infrastructure, testing, and partner integrations. Individual assignments and time commitments will be finalized with the delivery team.

**Funding and relationships:** The initiative has a proposed total budget of $267,000, with $200,000 sought from TheDAO and $67,000 expected to be raised through external contributions. The Ethereum Foundation is a prospective funding source, but no contribution has been committed or received specifically for this initiative. SEAL operates existing intelligence and incident-response infrastructure and maintains relationships throughout the Ethereum ecosystem. Any previously funded work or overlapping expenditures will be disclosed to avoid duplicate reimbursement.
sections.why_grant:
SEAL Intel builds on an established operational threat intelligence program rather than creating a new intelligence organization from scratch. SEAL already receives threat information through incident response, ecosystem reporting channels, security research, and trusted relationships with blockchain organizations. The grant will fund the incremental engineering, automation, intelligence processing, and integrations needed to turn those existing capabilities into a more scalable intelligence service.

**Existing foundation and grant-funded additions**

| Existing SEAL capability | Additional work funded by this grant |
|---|---|
| Incident and intelligence intake through SEAL reporting channels | Connect selected intake workflows to a shared intelligence pipeline, preserving source provenance and sharing permissions |
| Existing analyst research and threat intelligence workflows | Automate selected collection, normalization, deduplication, enrichment, and correlation tasks |
| Existing OpenCTI-related intelligence capabilities | Build and document additional integrations, Ethereum-specific data conventions, and production workflows |
| Public security research, intelligence reports, and malicious-domain contributions | Produce consistent, evidence-linked records, actionable recommendations, and machine-readable distribution |
| Established relationships with ecosystem organizations | Support integrations and independently verified operational adoption of the new intelligence feeds |

**Existing operational capabilities and track record**

- **Ecosystem intelligence network:** SEAL maintains more than 100 communication channels and hotlines connecting DeFi protocols, centralized exchanges, infrastructure providers, and other blockchain organizations. These relationships provide direct visibility into incidents and emerging threats.

- **24/7 incident and intelligence intake:** SEAL operates `@seal_911_bot` and `@seal_tips_bot`, supporting incident reporting, intelligence submissions, initial response coordination, and information sharing.

- **Phishing detection and blocklisting:** SEAL reports identifying approximately 5,000–10,000 malicious frontends weekly and contributes intelligence to ecosystem phishing blocklists. Its integration with MetaMask's eth-phishing-detect helps malicious frontends become blocked rapidly after identification.

- **Malware and threat actor research:** SEAL investigates DPRK-linked threat actors, malware-as-a-service operations, social engineering campaigns, malicious infrastructure, and software supply-chain compromises. Research outputs include indicators of compromise, attacker tactics and techniques, campaign analysis, and coordinated defensive actions.

- **Public intelligence and research:** SEAL publishes threat research, incident analysis, and operational statistics through SEAL Radar and maintains public research repositories and datasets.

- **Existing intelligence infrastructure:** SEAL already conducts structured intelligence research and maintains OpenCTI-related capabilities for organizing and analyzing threat information.

These capabilities give SEAL a significant operational advantage: direct incident visibility, researchers who understand both traditional cybersecurity and Ethereum-specific threats, and established relationships with organizations positioned to act on intelligence.

**Why grant funding is needed**

While SEAL already collects and analyzes intelligence, many processes still require manual collection, reconciliation, enrichment, and distribution. This grant will connect existing workflows, automate repeatable processing tasks, improve intelligence quality and consistency, and provide integrations that enable security teams to consume and act on intelligence more efficiently.

**Public evidence and references**

- SEAL Radar: https://radar.securityalliance.org/
- SEAL GitHub: https://github.com/security-alliance
- Lazarus Group research: https://lazarus.group/
- Public Lazarus intelligence dataset: https://github.com/security-alliance/lazarus-group-data
- Binance incident research: https://radar.securityalliance.org/tradertraitor-vs-contagious-interview-a-look-at-binances-initial-incident-report/
- DPRK malware research: https://radar.securityalliance.org/vs-code-tasks-abuse-by-contagious-interview-dprk/
- Weekly operational statistics: https://radar.securityalliance.org/seal-weekly-stats-20-27-oct-2026/
sections.commitments:
SEAL will deliver the agreed grant-funded capabilities and provide independently verifiable evidence against the approved milestones. Evidence will include documented source integrations, intelligence-processing workflows, analyst review procedures, distribution mechanisms, and operational adoption by independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations.

**Long-term sustainability:** SEAL intends to maintain the capabilities developed through this initiative as part of its existing intelligence operations after the six-month grant period. Sustainability will be supported through continued ecosystem funding and a proposed enhanced Intel/ISAC donor offering, currently envisioned at $50,000 annually per participating organization. The proposed offering would provide participating organizations with access to SEAL Intel services, including invitation-only private intelligence briefings, quarterly threat intelligence reports, and relevant intelligence feeds and alerts. This model is prospective and does not represent committed revenue.

**Public-good outputs and access:** Grant-funded public-good deliverables will be distinguished from additional donor-supported services. Intelligence involving sensitive incidents, private sources, or confidential reporting will remain subject to contributor permissions, confidentiality requirements, and applicable TLP restrictions.

**Licensing:** SEAL will specify the licenses and publication commitments applicable to grant-funded software, documentation, schemas, and other deliverables in the final grant agreement. Restricted intelligence and confidential source material will not be publicly released where doing so would violate applicable permissions.

**Maintenance:** Named maintainers, the minimum post-grant support period, and the operating budget required to sustain the funded capabilities will be confirmed before the grant agreement is finalized.

**Measurement and accountability:** The initiative will be evaluated against agreed quantitative milestones covering source integration, normalization, automated extraction accuracy, analyst productivity, alert delivery, intelligence distribution, and independent partner adoption. Public evidence will be provided where appropriate, with sensitive information redacted or made available to the independent reviewer through approved access arrangements.

Any exceptions concerning source-code publication, restricted intelligence, or other standard grant requirements will be expressly disclosed and agreed before implementation.

milestones.name: Data ingestion and normalization
criteria: 100% of ingested items are stored as STIX 2.1 bundles, including Ethereum-specific indicators such as addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, and malicious dApp domains.
Automated connectors/data feeds run in production for at least 10 sources across at least 5 source classes, and the source list is provided to the reviewer.
On a test set of 50 unstructured reports, automated extraction recovers at least 90% of the indicators identified by an analyst performing manual review.
At least 50% of observables ingested over a 14-day period are linked to an entity, such as a threat actor, campaign, malware family, or incident, rather than remaining standalone observables.
An automated overlap report runs at least daily for 14 consecutive days, identifying matches between newly ingested external intelligence and SEAL's privately gathered data.

milestones.name: Correlation, analyst workflows and alert delivery
criteria: Median analyst time required to produce a report through the new workflow is at least 50% lower than the manual baseline, measured using 10 reports against five baseline reports timed at the beginning of the grant.
Over a 30-day period, every alert for a relevant threat reaches participants within 24 hours of detection.
At least two intelligence reports per month containing defensive recommendations are produced through the new workflow and distributed. Report volume may vary depending on incident activity.
Authenticated TAXII 2.1 and REST endpoints are operational, and an external test client can retrieve intelligence filtered by threat category, participant type, and TLP level.

Recommendation templates are available for different participant profiles, including protocols, infrastructure providers, wallets, exchanges, security firms, government organizations, and institutional participants, with one issued example of each.
The partner onboarding guide, API reference, and TLP handling policy are published.

milestones.name: Partner adoption pilot
criteria: At least six independent organizations, representing at least three participant types, each retrieve intelligence from the feed or API on at least 20 days within a 30-day period, verified through access logs.
At least four of those organizations provide written confirmation that the TAXII or REST feed has been integrated into their own security tooling.
At least four of those organizations each contribute intelligence that becomes a released record.

At least three organizations provide written confirmation of a specific defensive action taken because of an alert or recommendation, such as blocking malicious infrastructure, rotating credentials, patching a vulnerability, or coordinating a takedown.
At least six additional organizations are onboarded and actively retrieving intelligence after the initial pilot cohort, with at least two joining in each of the final two months.
